title: Difficulties and dilemmas
subtitle: snag, stumbling block, gruelling, in a fix
summary: Grade a difficulty exactly - from a glitch or a snag to an ordeal - and handle the adjectives and informal idioms English uses for trouble.

lesson.heading: Nouns for difficulties, from small to serious
rows: a fairly small difficulty; both are general
a fairly small difficulty, usually a technical one
something that prevents action or agreement
an unexpected difficulty; often used in the plural
anything that stops progress, literally or metaphorically
something that prevents free action, progress or movement
a situation where a difficult choice must be made between two, sometimes unpleasant, alternatives
a severe experience that is very difficult, painful or tiring

lesson.heading: Choosing the right noun
lesson.text: The strength of the word matters. A **glitch** is a small technical annoyance; a **snag** is the one drawback in an otherwise good plan; a **stumbling block** brings negotiations to a halt; an **ordeal** is something you will write a book about afterwards.

examples.text: At first there were some **glitches** with the software, but it's OK now.
The proposal is very good. The only **snag** is that it is a little expensive.
Negotiations were going well until the issue of sick pay became a major **stumbling block**.
The hostage is writing a book about his six-month **ordeal**.
Mark used to have a speech **impediment**, but he's overcome it and is now an actor.

lesson.heading: Adjectives of difficulty and their collocations
rows: difficult to understand because it has many parts
unreasonably long and hard to follow
difficult to bear because it is annoying or uncomfortable
difficult to deal with or do
changeable, selfish and/or hard to control

lesson.text: **Difficulty** stays singular in the expression **to have difficulty in doing something**: I had great **difficulty in finding** a job at first - not ~~great difficulties~~.

lesson.heading: Informal complaints
lesson.text: Everyday English has a rich store of complaints. **What a pain!** and **What a drag!** both mean 'What a nuisance!' A **chore** is a boring job that has to be done, and **hassle** is a situation causing trouble - as a verb, to **hassle** someone is to ask them again and again.

examples.text: Oh dear, more homework! **What a pain!** / **What a drag!**
The software is good for editing still images, but editing video is a real **chore**.
I can't face the **hassle** of moving house again.
My daughter keeps **hassling** me for a new bike.
Having to listen to him singing is sheer **torture**!

lesson.heading: What's eating him? Working and struggling
lesson.text: To ask what is wrong with someone informally: **What's eating him?** / **What's got into him?** / **What's bugging him?** / **What's (up) with him?** To work extremely hard: **slog your guts out**, **grind**, **graft**, or **flog yourself to death**.

examples.text: **What's got into** you, Dan? You look really fed up!
I've been **slogging my guts out** at work and it's all getting too much.
My wife says I should leave rather than go on **flogging myself to death**.

lesson.heading: In trouble and out of it
rows: in a fix / in a spot / in a hole
up against it / up to your neck
in a difficult situation, with too much to deal with
off the hook / in the clear / out of the wood(s)
lesson.note: The downside of living here is the traffic thundering by.

exercises.prompt: Shona is caught in a terrible ___ - should she move abroad with the man she loves or take the promotion she has been offered at work?
exercises.explanation: A dilemma is a situation where a difficult choice has to be made between two alternatives.

exercises.prompt: At first there were some ___ with the software, but it's OK now.
exercises.explanation: A glitch is a small difficulty, usually a technical one.

exercises.prompt: Removing old files from my hard drive was a real ___ - I spent four boring hours doing it!
exercises.hint: (a boring job that must be done)
exercises.explanation: A chore is a boring job that has to be done.

exercises.prompt: The hostage is writing a book about his six-month ___.
exercises.explanation: An ordeal is a severe experience which is very difficult, painful or tiring.

exercises.prompt: The proposal is very good. The only ___ is that it is a little expensive.
exercises.explanation: A snag or a hitch is a fairly small, general difficulty.

exercises.prompt: The leaflet gives new businesses information about typical ___ to avoid.
exercises.explanation: A pitfall is an unexpected difficulty, and the word is often used in the plural.

exercises.prompt: Negotiations were going well until the issue of sick pay became a major ___.
exercises.explanation: A stumbling block is something that prevents action or agreement.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation with the adjective that describes it.

pairs.left: a pupil who deliberately makes it hard for his teacher to teach
an accident which affects the victim psychologically
a book that deals with very difficult ideas without simplifying them
a child who is very disobedient and self-willed
pain that is almost impossible to put up with
a speech whose line of argument is long and hard to follow

exercises.prompt: Which adjective best describes an exhausting Arctic expedition?
exercises.explanation: Gruelling means extremely tiring and difficult; arduous and tough are also possible here.

exercises.prompt: Which adjective best describes a decision that is not easy to make?
exercises.explanation: Tough collocates with decision, time, job and climate - difficult to deal with or do.

exercises.prompt: What's got ___ you, Dan? You look really fed up!
exercises.explanation: What's got into you? is an informal way of asking what is the matter.

exercises.prompt: I've been slogging my ___ out at work and it's all getting too much.
exercises.explanation: To slog your guts out is to work extremely hard.

exercises.prompt: My wife says I should leave rather than go on flogging myself to ___.
exercises.explanation: To flog yourself to death is to work far too hard.

exercises.prompt: I really can't face the ___ of looking for something else at the moment.
exercises.explanation: Hassle is a situation causing trouble or difficulty.

exercises.prompt: I'm having great ___ in finding somewhere else to live.
exercises.explanation: To have difficulty in doing something - always singular, never great difficulties.

exercises.prompt: That's the ___ of living in Cambridge - it's beautiful but accommodation is so expensive.
exercises.explanation: The downside of a situation is its disadvantage.

exercises.prompt: I hope you soon get through all your work and begin to feel off the ___.
exercises.explanation: To be off the hook, in the clear or out of the woods is to be freed from a difficult situation.

exercises.prompt: Does each expression mean you are in trouble or out of it?

exercises.answer: Studying for the exam was sheer torture
exercises.explanation: Torture is used figuratively for a very unpleasant experience.
